paper_title: GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: For more than half a century, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay. Generative video models (VMs) now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a VM turns the engine's coarse proxy video into final frames. These systems, however, treat the VM as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer. We present GameWM, a design for next-generation games built on a clear division of labor. The GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact: rules, state, camera, and the layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember it. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand: the look of the world and the detail of the player's interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, we build GameWM as a complete system: a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions enter the model, and a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play. Together they give every player a fresh version of the same game: each player's own character, world, and skills turn the same engine mechanics into a new experience, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed.

sections.content: Stable world Customized interaction More than just renderer Figure 1 One mechanic, customized realizations. The GameWM-engine defines one attack mechanic; the GameWM-VM realizes it as each characters own skill in that characters own world. GameWM Technical Report 1. Introduction game is series of interesting choices. Sid Meier Video games began as laboratory curiosities, Tennis for Two in 1958 and Spacewar! in 1962, and became an industry with Pong and the Magnavox Odyssey in 1972. Today 3.6B people play them [Newzoo, 2025]. Across these seven decades, successive generations of hardware and software have pursued the same three goals: better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay (Section 2). Progress on one axis has repeatedly opened the others. Hardware 3D acceleration made first-person shooters and open worlds possible. Networking turned games into persistent shared worlds. Accessible creation tools let players build and share worlds of their own. Generative video models are the newest technology to touch all three axes. On graphics, neural networks already produce most of the pixels in shipped games, although not yet through video generation: DLSS 4 upscales and interpolates frames so that 15 of every 16 displayed pixels are generated [NVIDIA, 2025c], DLSS 4.5 raises that to 23 of 24, and DLSS 5, released in September 2026, adds neural rendering stage that infuses engine frames with photoreal lighting and materials [NVIDIA, 2026a,b]. In parallel, open video models have grown from Wan2.1 (1.3B and 14B, February 2025) [Wan Team, 2025] to MiniMax H3 (33B, August 2026) [MiniMax, 2026], and their visual quality now approaches that of film footage. The open question is therefore no longer whether generated pixels belong in games, but how much of the game VM should be responsible for. On interaction, we distinguish two levels of semantic granularity. Coarse-grained interaction moves the camera and the protagonist through the world: where to look and where to go. Fine-grained interaction is what the protagonist does to an object or another character and how: opening car door and getting in, striking an opponent, casting spell. World models have gone through two generations, and both have centered on the coarse level (Section 3). The first is driven by low-dimensional action signals, camera poses or handful of keys [Bruce et al., 2024; He et al., 2025; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Valevski et al., 2024], and does not yet deliver even coarse-grained control: key says which way to go, but how fast the protagonist moves and how fast the camera turns are left to the model, so the same input yields different motion from one sample to the next. Because the world state lives only in generated frames, control degrades further under fast viewpoint changes and revisited places drift [Xiao et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026]. game built this way cannot be steered reliably, let alone played with immersive control. The second generation conditions the VM on proxy video: an engine, increasingly one written by coding agent, keeps the state and renders coarse proxy, and the VM turns it into the final frames [Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026c; Lu et al., 2026b; Matrix-Game Team, 2026; Zhan et al., 2026]. Because the proxy fixes layout and camera frame by frame and is re-rendered whenever the player returns, this route makes coarse-grained interaction exact and alleviates the memory problem, and it is becoming the mainstream for playable worlds. Fine-grained interaction, where new gameplay lies, has remained largely unexplored. Secondgeneration world models cast the VM as renderer: they pair each proxy with frames that game engine rendered or camera recorded [Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026c; Matrix-Game Team, 2026; Zhan et al., 2026], so proxy has exactly one correct output, and none of these systems treats protagonist interaction as the objective of data curation. Appearance may be restyled, but what happens and how it moves is fixed by the pair, which leaves most of the VMs generative capacity unused. Consider ranged attack. The engine resolves the mechanic exactly: who attacks, which target is hit at which frame, and how much damage is dealt; how the attack looks is not part of the mechanic. VM could realize the same event as fireball, an ice lance, or bolt of lightning, or as 2 GameWM Technical Report pistol shot or rifle burst, with the attackers motion following the weapon: staff is raised and swung, bow is drawn and released, rifle is shouldered and recoils. renderer cannot, because its data never pairs one proxy event with more than one realization. This is the increment VM can bring to game: not restyled copy of the engines frames, but fine-grained interactions that the engine never animated, played out on outcomes that the engine still computes. Because the realization follows the players own character, world, and skills, the same mechanics unfold as different interactions for every player, and each player meets their own version of the game. On gameplay, existing work is even less concrete. position paper proposes interactive generative video as the basis of generative game engine and outlines five-level maturity roadmap [Yu et al., 2025a]. Matrix-Game 4.0 [Matrix-Game Team, 2026] lets coding agent create gameplay from natural language, Magpie [Zhan et al., 2026] targets the prototyping stage of game development, and Project Genie [Google, 2026] offers 60-second explorable worlds but, by Googles own account, is not game engine [Vigliarolo, 2026]. These works describe what generative games could be, but not what VM adds to game that its engine cannot: session is specified by prompt, first frame, or an engine scene, and who the protagonist is, what world it lives in, and what it can do are left unspecified. We present GameWM, system design for next-generation games in which the VM is first-class component with defined responsibility. Building on the engineVM split of proxy-conditioned systems [Chen et al., 2026], GameWM names the two sides the GameWM-engine and the GameWMVM and designs every part of the system around the contract between them: division of labor, an authoring interface through which game supplies its characters, scenes, and skills, data engine curated for interactions, model family that implements the GameWM-VM for offline content and real-time play, and an evaluation that sets every output beside the proxy that drove it and the event timing. The GameWM-engine is defined by this contract rather than by an implementation: any engine, hand-written or produced by coding agent, fills the role if it supplies what it computes exactly and cheaply, namely rules, state, camera, layout, and the coarse kinematics of the protagonist and the objects it interacts with, as proxy video and log of events. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author: the appearance of the world and the articulated detail of protagonist interactions, and it may realize one engine event in many ways as long as the events semantics are preserved. game is then authored as rules in the GameWM-engine plus character sheet, scene concept art, and skill descriptions that the GameWM-VM renders. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: system design that assigns the VM responsibility. The design splits game into GameWMengine, specified by the contract it must meet, and GameWM-VM, and turns the VM from renderer into the source of fresh, personal experience for every player: the same mechanics, played as the players own character, in the players own world, with the players own skills, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed. This places GameWM between proxy renderers, which only restyle the motion the engine authored, and pure world models, which fail to maintain stable world. An interaction-centric data engine. It mines interaction-rich clips from unpacked game buffers and from screen recordings of many titles, and turns them into aligned pairs with four proxy modalities, stylized targets, interaction-centric captions, and VLM-based quality control. Proxies of screen recordings come from monocular estimates rather than engine access, so any footage can enter and target appearance is not bounded by any one engine. model family from 5B to 33B that implements the GameWM-VM. All members share one proxy-reference interface trained with LoRA or full fine-tuning, without extra control modules, 3 GameWM Technical Report and are mapped to deployment tiers: GameWM-H3-33B for offline content and as the distillation teacher, GameWM-Wan2.2-14B as low-cost offline model, and causal GameWM-Wan2.2-5B for real-time play; GameWM-H3-33B is also distilled into four-step causal model that generates chunk by chunk. We evaluate them visually on held-out interaction clips, with every output shown beside the proxy that drove it and the recorded event times marked. 2. Seven Decades of Video Games along Three Axes Figure 2 Seven decades of games along graphics, interaction, and gameplay. Eras are delimited by transitions in graphics, and each dated landmark is placed in the era of its release. Interaction is split as in Section 1: coarse-grained interaction moves the camera and the protagonist; fine-grained interaction is what the protagonist does to objects and characters. Across the eras of Figure 2, one cycle repeats in three steps, and it tells us where VM should sit in game. machine takes over one stage of authoring. Real-time 3D replaced hand-drawn sprites, shaders and ray tracing compute lighting that artists once baked, physics middleware and motion matching move the objects and bodies once scripted or keyed, and DLSS reconstructs most of the pixels the engine once shaded. Coarse-grained control has needed no new takeover since the mid-1990s. Finegrained interaction is still authored per character: every action the protagonist can perform on an object or character, and how it looks, is designed in advance. This is the stage VM can take over. 4 GameWM Technical Report The machine joins the engine under contract. None of these steps replaced the engine. Each came with contract, such as middleware interfaces, or for DLSS 5 an engine frame that defines what must remain [NVIDIA, 2026b], and the engine stayed authoritative over content and rules. Pure world models instead ask the industry to replace the engine, its rules, and its tools at once; Google spokesperson has said that Genie is not game engine and cant create full game experience [Vigliarolo, 2026]. GameWM keeps the engine and makes the contract explicit: the GameWM-engine computes every event, and the GameWM-VM decides how it plays out. The new capacity becomes new gameplay. Real-time 3D brought open worlds, physics brought puzzles and combat built on objects, and systemic objects brought the emergent play of Breath of the Wild. DLSS makes games look better but leaves their play unchanged, and so does VM used only as renderer. Because fine-grained interaction is authored once per character, every player sees the same actions; VM that takes over this stage can realize them anew for each player, as the players own character with the players own skills (Section 4.3). 3. GameWM System Design GameWM is designed for one experience: an immersive game in which the players own character, weapons, and skills look the same and change the world in the same way in every clip, scene, and session, while every rule and outcome stays exact. This section derives the system from that goal. Section 4.1 places GameWM between engine-bound graphics and pure world models, Section 4.2 divides each frame between the GameWM-engine and the GameWM-VM, and Section 4.3 shows how game is authored once so that what the GameWM-VM generates stays consistent. The models that take these assets as input, and the deployment tiers they serve, follow in Section 6. 4.1. Where GameWM Sits: Stability and Generative Capability From traditional graphics to pure world model, each design hands one more module of the frame to neural network (Figure 3). DLSS takes over the final pixels and refines what the engine rendered [NVIDIA, 2025c, 2026b]. Proxy renderers, the engine-conditioned world models such as CWM, Magpie, PWM, and Matrix-Game 4.0, take over appearance and render it from coarse proxy video rather than from finished engine frames [Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026d; Matrix-Game Team, 2026; Zhan et al., 2026]. GameWM also hands over interaction detail: how each interaction plays out. Pure world models such as Genie 3 and LingBot-World hand over the rest, namely layout, motion, rules, and state [Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026]. Each step adds generative capability, the range of content the network produces without being authored, and gives up some game stability, the guarantee that rules, state, and outcomes are exact and replayable. Stability declines slowly while the engine keeps the world state, because visual error cannot change an outcome; it collapses once the state moves into the generated frames and outcomes become visual guesses. GameWM takes the last step before that collapse: it maximizes generative capability subject to game stability, with the network deciding how interactions look and the engine still deciding where everything is and what happens. 4.2. Division of Labor The GameWM-engine keeps everything designer must be able to inspect, replay, and balance: rules, scores, health, collisions, quest state, and the positions and coarse poses of all entities. It renders proxy video from the players camera. The proxy determines where things are and when an interaction happens, for example that the protagonist reaches the drivers door at second 2.1 and the car departs at second 3.4. The quantities on the GameWM-engine side are cheap to compute exactly and expensive for VM to infer: rule is line of code, and revisit is re-render. The quantities on the GameWM-VM side are expensive to author and cheap to sample from strong prior: new interaction costs an animator weeks, but VM trained on interaction footage has seen thousands of examples of people entering cars. One event, many realizations. Because outcomes live in the GameWM-engine, the GameWM-VM is free to vary everything that does not change them. An engine event fixes its semantics, such as the event type, the participants, and the hit frame, together with the coarse kinematics of the bodies involved; any realization that keeps these is valid, so one ranged attack can appear as fire spell, an ice spell, or rifle shot. The proxy therefore has to carry event semantics rather than fully posed animation, and the data has to pair one event type with many realizations (Section 5.2). Section 4.3 uses this freedom to give every character its own skills. 4.3. Authored Once: Consistency for an Immersive Game What GameWM offers the player is immersion, and immersion rests on consistency. player who plays fire mage expects the same face and costume in every scene, the same fire in every attack, and the same scorch where that fire lands; if any of these changes from one clip to the next, the game stops feeling like one world. Game world models so far set up each session from prompt, first frame, or an engine scene, and nothing in the system carries the protagonists identity or abilities from one session to the next. Mechanics from the GameWM-engine. The game framework defines small set of mechanics, for example melee attack, ranged attack, and dash. Each is code with exact rules: what can be targeted, when the hit lands, and how much damage it does. The designer writes each mechanic once, every character shares it, and it is what the proxy shows: coarse bodies in motion and an event in the engines log. The character and its world. character sheet shows the protagonist from the front, the side, and the back. In conventional production character is textured, rigged 3D model with an animation set. Under the division of labor this asset splits in two: the GameWM-engine keeps coarse body, capsule or low-poly mesh that it simulates, collides, and renders into the proxy, and the sheet carries everything the player sees, at the cost of an image instead of modeling, rigging, and animation. The first frame, scene concept art aligned with the GameWM-engines opening view, sets the look of the world. The two are generated to agree with each other, starting from whichever the player provides. From sheet, an image model paints the first frame from that opening view with the character in it; this is the step that restyles first frames in the data engine, so the anchor relates to the proxy at inference as it did in training. From first frame, the image model draws sheet of its protagonist. The sheet slot is trained with exact supervision, because each stylized target in the data engine was rendered from its sheet (Section 5.3), and the sheet is dropped for fifth of those samples, so the first frame alone can also set both the world and the protagonist. Skills: mechanic attribute. character also implies how it fights. High-level attributes are read from the sheet, such as an element, weapon, and palette, and each attribute is fused with each engine mechanic into one entry of the characters skill tree. For the fire mage, the melee attack becomes Flame Fist, the ranged attack Fireball, and the dash Ember Dash; an ice mage on the same mechanics gets frost versions of all three. Each entry is text that describes the skills look, including what it does to the scene, such as the burst on impact or the embers left on the ground. designer 9 GameWM Technical Report thus writes each mechanic once and obtains family of skills across characters, and player can wield skills that no artist animated. From assets to frames. At run time the GameWM-engine turns the players input into proxy frames and resolves each event exactly. When an event uses mechanic, the characters entry for that mechanic is added to the caption of the chunk in which it occurs, and the first frame, the sheet, the proxy chunk, and the caption enter the GameWM-VM together as in-context references (Section 6.2): motion, framing, and positions follow the proxy, the worlds look follows the first frame, the protagonists identity follows the sheet, and the caption describes the event. The GameWM-engine still decides the target, the hit frame, and the damage; the entry decides only how the skill looks, and the GameWMVM generates the attackers motion, the projectile, the impact, and the targets reaction in step with the hit frame. Together these assets make the experience consistent across game rather than within clip: the same protagonist appears in every scene, each scene opens with its authored look, every use of skill draws on the same description, and its timing and outcome come from the same engine rule. Interaction-Centric Data Engine Figure 5 summarizes the data engine. clip comes from one of two sources: game recording whose depth, semantics, player state, and event tags are read from engine buffers, or screen recording of another title, whose depth and semantics are estimated by monocular models [Kong et al., 2026; Ravi et al., 2025] and whose events are tagged by VLM. Clips are cut around interactions and reduced to three proxy modalities (DUV, depth, and semantics) and window-scoped event caption. H3s reference-to-video-and-audio mode (Ref2VA) then renders each clip again from its semantic video and event text: 𝑚 low-poly versions, which stand in for the proxy frames GameWM-engine would render, such as simple engine or one written by coding agent, and serve as further proxies, and 𝑛 high-fidelity versions, which take their look from restyled first frame and an optional character sheet and serve, with the source recording, as targets. 5.1. Sources and the Appearance Ceiling Paired data captured inside an engine has an appearance ceiling: the target is itself an engine render, so model trained on it learns to look like that engine. GameWM therefore does not tie its data to one engine. Any footage from which per-frame depth and semantics can be obtained, either read from engine buffers or estimated by monocular models, enters the same pipeline and is reduced to the same proxy interface: per-frame depth and semantics, also packed into single RGB video (DUV), and low-poly re-renders in four styles (amateur low-poly, capsules, Blender primitives, and MagicaVoxel), which show the structure of scene without the engines appearance. Appendix gives the encoding. Adding source requires only an extractor; the training interface does not change. Figure 6 shows the sources currently converted and the events their clips carry, divided by granularity. 5.2. Fine-Grained Curation and Coarse Expansion The sources play two roles, and they are curated differently. Fine-grained events teach interactions. Where the source reports what happens, clips are cut around events rather than sampled uniformly. In the GTA recordings the engine reports each event, 10 GameWM Technical Report Figure 5 The interaction-centric data engine. Left: both source paths yield the same three proxies and an event caption, from which H3 Ref2VA renders 𝑚 low-poly and 𝑛 high-fidelity versions of the clip. After VLM screening, each of the three proxies and the 𝑚 low-poly videos is paired with every high-fidelity target and with the source recording. Right: one enter vehicle clip with 𝑚 = 𝑛 = 4, giving 7 4 = 28 stylized pairs, plus seven with the recording (not drawn); the outlined cell is the pair shown above the grid. such as enter_vehicle or shoot, with its frame, and the event times enter the proxy and the caption. Fine-grained events have participant and key frame that decides the outcome: entering or exiting vehicle, melee hit, shot. They are what the GameWM-VM cannot infer from motion alone and what the GameWM-engines clock must time. Coarse events are locomotion modes, such as driving, swimming, or climbing, which the proxy already describes almost completely. Of the 1,460 GTA clips in the snapshot, 1,018 (70%) are fine-grained (Figure 6, right); Figure 7 shows one training pair per event. Coarse and untagged clips broaden appearance. ABot-World, Magpie, and CARLA tag only locomotion or nothing, so their clips cannot be cut around events, but they reduce to the same proxy interface and are rendered into the same target styles. With the coarse GTA clips they make up 84% of the corpus and supply far more scenes, layouts, and camera paths than one game offers, from which the model learns to take structure from the proxy and appearance from the anchor (Section 4.3). Interactions are thus learned from the fine-grained part, and appearance transfer from all of it. One event can also look many ways. Captions name the realization (weapon, element, vehicle class) so that text can select it, but recorded realizations are still few: melee is bare-handed, and the vehicles are cars and helicopter. Others, such as spell elements and melee weapons, are supplied at inference by the character sheet and the skill text (Figure 9). 5.3. Diverse Targets and Verified Captions proxy describes structure; the target and the caption decide what the model learns to put on top of it. clips targets are its source recording and its high-fidelity renders. Each render takes the semantic proxy, first frame restyled by an image model, and, for many renditions, character sheet 11 GameWM Technical Report Figure 6 Composition of the data engine by source clips. Left: the share of each source. Right: the event of every clip, with granularity on the inner ring and the event on the outer ring; hue gives the source, and height the granularity (fine-grained, coarse, untagged). ABot-World is the released 500-hour, action-annotated part of the training data of ABot-World-0 [ABot-World Team, 2026], with depth and semantics estimated by MoGe-3 [Kong et al., 2026] and SAM 2 [Ravi et al., 2025]; CARLA [Dosovitskiy et al., 2017] and Magpie [Zhan et al., 2026] come from SolarRenderer-Data [Fang et al., 2026]. Shares are of the snapshot in Table 6. showing the protagonist or the driven vehicle from the front, the side, and the back. The renders subject is drawn from that sheet, so the sheet is an exact identity reference for it and is kept with the pair; the source recording has none. Pairing one proxy with targets of different looks forces the model to take structure from the proxy and appearance from the anchor and the sheet. Each 5.17 training window gets its own caption with timestamp prefixes. Because captioners describe objects that scene usually contains, the per-second content of the proxy is given to the captioner as prior and used to check its reply: caption that mentions car in second without vehicle pixels fails (Appendix A). 5.4. Quality Control Follows Provenance Proxies are checked only where they are estimated. Depth and semantics read from engine buffers or from simulator (GTA V, CARLA, Magpie) are exact; those estimated from screen recordings can flicker or mislabel over time, so these clips are reviewed by VLM for the temporal stability and accuracy of depth and semantics. Every rendered video, low-poly or high-fidelity, is generated and is therefore screened: VLM compares it with its source clip on camera, motion and timing, spatial relations, style, and, with sheet, identity, and human reviewer can override any decision. Acceptance tracks the proxy  (Table 6)  : 94% of the GTA low-poly renders and 70% of its high-fidelity renders pass, against about half or less for renders built on estimated (ABot-World) or sparse gray-box (Magpie) proxies. Exact proxies thus pay twice: they need no screening themselves, and the targets built on them are more reliable. Appendix gives the review panels, the axes, the decision rules, and the rates per source. 12 GameWM Technical Report Figure 7 One training pair per engine event. Each block shows clips capsule re-render, which is the proxy, above the source recording. The first two rows are fine-grained GTA events; the rest are coarse or untagged clips from GTA V, Magpie, ABot-World, and CARLA. Red ticks mark engine state changes. The capsules carry the camera, the layout, and the timing of each event, but no limbs, faces, or effects. 13 GameWM Technical Report 6. The GameWM Model Family 6.1. Deployment Tiers models scale decides where it can run, and where it runs decides what it can serve. GameWM is therefore family of three models, one per deployment tier, rather than one model. The offline tier, GameWM-H3-33B, has the highest quality. It renders cutscenes, trailers, player replays, and user-generated videos, produces training data, and serves as the teacher for distillation. single H3 stream currently takes several datacenter GPUs, so this tier is not for live play. The player tier, causal GameWM-Wan2.2-5B, is distilled to few-step chunk-wise generation for real-time play. Matrix-Game 4.0 shows that 5B renderer can reach 60 FPS at 480p on one RTX 5090 [Matrix-Game Team, 2026], so this is the tier that can follow DLSS onto consumer hardware. GameWM-Wan2.2-14B sits between the two as low-cost offline model. It serves offline content that does not need the quality of the 33B model at fraction of its cost, and it is the platform on which data and design choices are screened before they are run at 33B. 6.2. Interface and Backbones All GameWM models share one interface. The inputs enter through the backbones existing reference pathway rather than new control branch: the proxy video as <Video 1>, the first frame as <Picture 1>, the optional character sheet as <Picture 2>, and text that states each inputs role and describes the event. One model accepts four proxy modalities, distinguished by modality tag in the text: packed depth and semantics (DUV), depth, semantics, and low-poly re-renders. Backbones are adapted with LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] or full fine-tuning only. Proxy frames are placed either as sequential prefix or at the temporal coordinates (in the rotary position embedding [Su et al., 2021]) of the target frames they describe; Appendix C.1 compares the two. The models differ in backbone and in how the proxy enters it. GameWM-H3-33B places the proxy in H3s native Ref2VA reference rows and trains rank-128 LoRA on the attention projections; the audio rows are kept but receive zero loss. GameWM-Wan2.2-14B is built on the high-noise expert of Wan2.2-I2V-A14B, which runs every denoising step (the low-noise expert is not used), and trains rank-128 LoRA on the attention projections at 832 480 and 81 frames at 16 fps. GameWM-Wan2.25B is built on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and is fully fine-tuned at 1280 704 and 121 frames at 24 fps. Wan2.2 has no reference slot, so the inputs of the shared interface are laid out as one token sequence for its self-attention: the pictures (first frame, then the sheet), the proxy, and the target, each patchified on its own spatial grid. The proxy is encoded at half the targets spatial resolution and placed as temporal prefix, i.e. its latent frames take the time coordinates after the pictures and before the target. Long Rollout and Real-Time Distillation Long sessions are generated in windows: the first window receives one latent frame of context, and later windows receive ten. CWM uses similar 34-frame overlap, so we only report the setting. All three models are distilled in the three stages of SolarWM [Huang et al., 2026a]: bidirectional adaptation, teacher-forced AnyFlow causal initialization, and DMD with self-gradient forcing, which yields four-step causal student per backbone. In the causal stages each chunk reads only its own proxy chunk and the five before it (Eq. (2)). Section 7.3 compares the three students on one clip. 7. Bidirectional Model One interaction, every proxy. Figure 8 drives one held-out vehicle entry with six proxies and static control. Under the three engine buffers the camera, the street, and the parked cars follow the proxy, and the protagonist reaches the door and is seated at the engines frames. The three coarse re-renders carry no limb motion, and under the capsules the protagonist is rigid body, yet in all three he runs to the car, the door opens, and the car pulls away on the engines schedule: the model decides how the interaction plays out (Figure 3). Matrix-Game 4.0 analyzes real-time deployment of 5B proxy-conditioned renderer in detail [Matrix-Game Team, 2026]. The proxy-position ablation and summary of scaling are in Appendix C. 8. Conclusion GameWM makes video model component of game rather than its replacement. The GameWMengine keeps the world and computes every event, and it hands each event to the GameWM-VM as coarse proxy video and an event log; the GameWM-VM decides how the event plays out, as the character and the skills authored for it. An interaction-centric data engine builds training pairs for this contract from game recordings, screen recordings, and simulator footage, and one interface carries it across backbones from 5B to 33B parameters. On held-out clips, the models complete each interaction on the engines schedule from proxies as coarse as capsules, realize one mechanic as the skills of many characters, and keep the timing after distillation into four-step causal students. 22 GameWM Technical Report

All sources are written in one format, whether depth and semantics come from engine buffers or from monocular estimates. Semantics use the twelve classes of CWMs released DUV format [Chen et al., 2026]; engine semantics arrive with the recordings own classes (five in the main GTA recordings: static world, sky, player, pedestrians, and vehicles) and are mapped onto them. In DUV, the channel stores inverse log depth over 0.3256 and the and channels store lattice code of the semantic class. DUV is encoded losslessly and verified bit by bit on read-back. Each low-poly style starts from first frame restyled into that style by an image model and is rendered by H3 Ref2VA from the clips semantic video and event text, as the high-fidelity targets are (Section 5). Render check. Each low-poly and high-fidelity render is compared with its source clip by Gemini [Google DeepMind, 2026] before it enters training. For game clips, whose proxies are exact, this is the only quality filter. The VLM scores separate axes: camera (trajectory, framing, and view angle), motion (action type, direction, and phase timing), spatial relations (layout and depth ordering of the subjects), and style (adherence to the requested look); renders with character sheet add identity, scored for every sheet subject, with the minimum over subjects as the axis score, and the current prompt adds scene layout, whether the static environment keeps the sources layout. Each axis returns score, confidence, tags such as viewpoint or unverifiable, and time-stamped evidence that pairs what the source shows with what the render shows. Each axis is scored from 0 to 4, and render passes only if every axis scores at least 3; rejected render is queued for human check, and an axis marked unverifiable, for example subject fully covered by mask, never counts as passed. Of 1,414 recent verdicts, 72% passed; in the rejects the failing axis was most often scene layout, followed by spatial relations, motion, camera, and style, and almost never identity. Pass rates per source are reported in Table 6: exact engine and simulator proxies give the highest rates (GTA V, and 75% of the CARLA low-poly renders), estimated depth and semantics (ABot-World) and sparse gray-box geometry (Magpie) about half or less. For GTA and ABot-World, high-fidelity renders pass less often than low-poly ones, since they must also hold the style and the identity of the anchor. Window-scoped captions. The captioner receives the clip, grid of time bins, and per-second evidence table decoded from the DUV proxy without any model call: the number of people and vehicles on screen, whether the protagonist is visible, the depth range, and whether anything moved. Its reply is small JSON document of observations; the caption text, its ordering, and the timestamps are rendered by code. The captioner selects bin indices rather than writing clock times, and names the protagonists facing in screen space from closed list, since free-form directions such as facing forward were read in opposite ways by writer and reader. malformed reply is returned to the captioner with the list of problems for one retry. Caption verification. Each caption is then held against the same evidence table. claim the proxy contradicts outright, such as vehicle in second with no vehicle pixels or protagonist in second with no protagonist pixels, is fail; disagreement with an innocent explanation, such as bystander count off by one or still subject while follow camera moves, is warn. Fails mark hallucinations, which would teach the model to generate objects the proxy does not ask for; warns are worth counting across the corpus but not worth dropping clip for. The two rates are tracked separately: rising fail rate means the captioner is losing its grip on the evidence, while rising warn rate usually means verification threshold needs to move. B. Evaluation Protocol No public benchmark yet exists for video generation referenced by proxy video. General benchmarks score visual quality or text alignment [Huang et al., 2024], and world-model benchmarks score actionconditioned navigation, memory, and multi-turn interaction [Lu et al., 2026a; Ye et al., 2026; Ying et al., 2026]; neither checks whether generated clip follows proxy frame by frame or completes the interaction the engine specified. Proxy-conditioned systems also differ in proxy format, resolution, and conditioning interface, so numbers measured on one systems proxies do not transfer to another. We therefore compare each output directly with its proxy on held-out clips and compare only our own models and checkpoints with each other. Held-out clips. Clips are split by source recording, so no recording contributes to both training and evaluation, and stratified by target type, proxy modality, and action. Subsets cover clips with engine-buffer proxies, screen recordings with estimated proxies, and fast camera motion. 31 GameWM Technical Report Visual comparison. The report relies on visual comparison rather than aggregate metrics. Every figure places the proxy above the output it drives on shared time columns and marks the engines event frames, so that adherence to layout and camera, the completion of an interaction, and its timing are judged frame by frame against the engine rather than against another model. Event times come from the engine record or, where none was kept, are read off the proxy; the frames at which the generated interaction happens are read off the output. Two quantities are measured where visual judgment would be ambiguous: protagonist identity, as DINOv2 [Oquab et al., 2023] similarity between the tracked protagonist and its character sheet  (Table 4)  , and latency  (Table 5)  . Identity metric. People are detected with DETR [Carion et al., 2020] every six frames, and the protagonist is tracked by box overlap from its box in the first proxy frame; track stops once the protagonist enters vehicle. The score is the cosine similarity between the DINOv2 CLS feature of each crop and the three views of the sheet, maximized over views since the protagonist mostly faces away, and averaged over the track. The same quantity averaged over the other three characters sheets is the cross-identity baseline. Comparisons.
